rv.q: But Mitchell proves that it still has the power to shock, not just in its attitude to violence but in its refusal to shy away from the furthest reaches of emotional despair.
Mitchell's production might leave you whimpering under your seat in distress, but in this play about love and systematic dehumanisation, the words "felt it" take on a kind of triumph.
For all the ferocity in which it traffics, this production, like the play itself, feels like a gesture of love.
I’ve rarely been so overwhelmed by a show, but I’ve also never longed so much for one to end.
Michelle Terry, on stage throughout, watches it all with steady intelligence.
Her production is simultaneously repellent and compelling.
The sadistic obsession with upfront ghastliness dominates everything and rather than harrowing the soul the show merely perturbs the senses.
